claims.text: Lower synthesis temperatures restrict atomic diffusion and adatom mobility during one-step colloidal preparation of PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Restricted atomic diffusion and adatom mobility favor homogeneous, entropy-driven PtPdCoCuNi alloy formation.
Homogeneous PtPdCoCuNi alloy formation produces well-isolated noble-metal active sites.
Well-isolated noble-metal sites improve nitrobenzene hydrogenation performance relative to material made under a higher-temperature condition.
The controlled comparison is between synthesis at 60–80 °C and synthesis at 120–150 °C with otherwise identical precursor concentrations and atmosphere.
DRIFTS and XPS can assess the degree of atomic intermixing in the synthesized nanoparticles.
TEM and DLS can establish whether particle-size or dispersion differences account for catalytic-performance differences.
Lower-temperature synthesis limits premature agglomeration and phase segregation.
Reduced agglomeration and phase segregation promote a randomized, entropy-favored alloy.
The randomized alloy creates isolated and electronically optimized noble-metal sites.
Isolated and electronically optimized noble-metal sites enhance charge transfer and catalytic efficiency.
Low-temperature samples will have a more uniform atomic distribution than high-temperature samples.
Low-temperature samples will give a higher nitrobenzene hydrogenation yield than high-temperature samples.
Low-temperature samples will have a lower activation barrier for nitrobenzene hydrogenation than high-temperature samples.
Higher-temperature synthesis permits increased atomic diffusion that may produce less homogeneous alloy formation and lower catalytic performance.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to one-step colloidal PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles in inert solvents, within 60–80 °C versus 120–150 °C conditions, for nitrobenzene hydrogenation.
Temperature may independently affect nucleation rate and particle size.
Failure of low-temperature samples to show statistically significant improvements in both atomic homogeneity and catalytic performance after accounting for particle size would falsify the hypothesis.
